clue.text: Politician involved in smear goes to earth in usual hangout

indicators.note: something involved in another is caught up inside it, so one word sits within the other

blocks.note: a smear is a stain or mark
Member of Parliament
taken loosely as a one-letter short form of go
earth and ground are synonyms; to go to ground or to earth is to hide

explanation.surface: A politician caught up in a smear campaign hides away in their favourite haunt.
explanation.walkthrough: The lone second G is loose: it seems to stand for goes, with 'to earth' echoing the idiom 'go to ground', meaning to hide.
explanation.definitionFit: A stamping ground is the place a person regularly frequents, an idiom for one's familiar haunt.

clue.text: BBC bring us production on career for cleaner

indicators.note: a production is something made up or staged, so these letters are put together in a new order

blocks.note: the letters as written, to be rearranged
to career is to rush along headlong

explanation.surface: A TV station's production about a cleaning career, perhaps a fly-on-the-wall documentary about a cleaner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Career' looks like a noun meaning a job, but here it is the verb: to career is to race along.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrubbing brush is a stiff-bristled tool used for cleaning floors and surfaces, so it is a cleaner.

clue.text: Senior officer takes Russian vehicle up to orbit space station

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards
to orbit something is to circle it, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: Lada is a Russian make of car
Mir was the Soviet and Russian space station

explanation.surface: A senior officer rides a Russian vehicle up into space to orbit a space station.
explanation.definitionFit: An admiral is a top-ranking naval officer, so a senior officer.

clue.text: Change coming over arch-criminal, perhaps?

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked, so these letters are bent into a new order
one thing coming over another covers it on both sides, so it surrounds it

blocks.note: pence are small coins, loose change
the word arch with its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Wondering whether an arch-criminal might have a change of heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arch-criminal' reads as one villain, but the hyphen splits: arch is the fodder and criminal its anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Perchance is an old-fashioned word for maybe, so it means perhaps.

clue.text: No point having feeling without meaning

definitions.note: adjectival phrase for a noun answer: what is nonsense is without meaning

blocks.note: taken as written
N is a compass point, north
a sense is a feeling or faculty of perception

explanation.surface: Having no point and no feeling: a sneer at something pointless and empty.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonsense is talk or writing that lacks sense, words that convey nothing.

clue.text: About time! Pull up at the side of the road

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from the bottom, backwards

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
T is the abbreviation for time
to tug is to pull

explanation.surface: An impatient driver finally gets someone to pull over at the roadside: about time!
explanation.walkthrough: 'About time!' reads as an exclamation, but it is two separate pieces; 'Pull up' likewise looks like stopping a car.
explanation.definitionFit: The gutter is the channel running along the edge of a road, so it lies at the side of the road.

clue.text: Get up and go very fast, heading off

indicators.note: with its heading removed, the first character is dropped

blocks.note: a hundred miles an hour is a very fast speed

explanation.surface: An instruction to get moving at great speed.
explanation.walkthrough: Write the speed as 100MPH, drop the leading 1, and read the two zeros as letter Os.
explanation.definitionFit: Oomph is energy and vigour, the same thing as get-up-and-go.

clue.text: Chosen one's born without honour at home

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so the other pieces go around

blocks.note: née marks a woman's name at birth
the Order of Merit, a British honour
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: A chosen candidate turns out to have been born without any honour in their own country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like lacking, but in its old sense it means outside. OM, the Order of Merit, is a British honour in the monarch's gift.
explanation.definitionFit: A nominee is a person put forward or selected for a post or award.

clue.text: Average man with debt gets crafty in a mean way

blocks.note: par is the normal or average level
a man's name
an IOU is a written acknowledgement of debt
sly means cunning or crafty

explanation.surface: An ordinary man in debt turns crafty and behaves stingily.
explanation.definitionFit: Parsimoniously means stingily, with extreme reluctance to spend money.

clue.text: Artist with US band has trademark shirt

blocks.note: R.E.M. was an American rock band
a brand is a trademark
T as in T-shirt

explanation.surface: An artist teams up with an American band whose shirts carry its trademark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shirt' gives only T, the letter that names the T-shirt.
explanation.definitionFit: Rembrandt was the great Dutch painter of the seventeenth century.

clue.text: A doctor's bitten by oddly mean snake

indicators.note: oddly keeps the letters in the first, third and other odd positions
what is bitten by something is held between its jaws, so it sits inside

blocks.note: the first and third letters
taken as written
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A doctor gets bitten by a particularly nasty snake.
explanation.definitionFit: The mamba is a venomous African snake, the black mamba being the best known.

clue.text: Knock up cradle with hardwood

indicators.note: knocked up in an across clue turns the word over so it reads backwards

blocks.note: a crib is a baby's cradle
the first half of this word, hard, is abbreviated H as on pencils; its second half is the definition

explanation.surface: A carpenter knocks up a baby's cradle out of hardwood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardwood' must be split: hard gives H and wood is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Birch is a tree and its timber, so a kind of wood.

clue.text: Animals long kept in pens hate going out

indicators.note: pens going out suggests the creatures escaping and scattering, so the letters break loose into a new order

blocks.note: L is an abbreviation for long
the letters as written

explanation.surface: Animals that have long been kept in enclosures hate being let out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kept in' is only scene-setting for the L joining the fodder; the whole lot is rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: Elephants are large mammals, so examples of animals.

clue.text: I'd take on student having seen disastrous results ending in laziness

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter
something disastrous is wrecked, so these letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written without the apostrophe
L for learner
taken as written, to be rearranged
the final letter

explanation.surface: A student has seen disastrous exam results, which they put down to their own laziness.
explanation.definitionFit: Idleness is the state of not working or being lazy, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Poor Master Brook

indicators.note: something in poor shape is badly made, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters as written

explanation.surface: It reads like a sad name tag: poor young Master Brook, a boy called Brook.
explanation.walkthrough: Brook looks like a surname after Master, the old title for a boy, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A brook is a small river, the same as a stream.

clue.text: Dodgy mushroom with toast's keeping daughter bent over toilet

indicators.note: one word keeping another holds it inside itself
something bent over is turned back on itself, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
D is the abbreviation for daughter
loo is British slang for toilet

explanation.surface: After eating a bad mushroom on toast, the daughter is left bent over the toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent over' looks like the daughter's posture, but it turns the toilet word backwards; loo is everyday British for toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A toadstool is a mushroom-like fungus regarded as poisonous, so a dodgy mushroom.

clue.text: Hanging back to see old bird get fish after diving, initially

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the word before it
after tells the solver to place the fish piece behind the piece from diving rather than before it

blocks.note: daw is the old name for the jackdaw
the opening letter
the ling is a long sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: Lingering to watch an old bird dive down and catch a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Daw is the old name for the jackdaw, a member of the crow family.
explanation.definitionFit: Dawdling is moving slowly and lagging behind, so hanging back.

clue.text: Bother to come back and fire French foreman

indicators.note: coming back means returning the way it came, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: a fag is British slang for a tiresome chore, a bother
fer is French, though for iron rather than fire

explanation.surface: A French foreman is told to come back and fire someone, with all the bother that brings.
explanation.walkthrough: The last three letters are loose: the French for fire is feu, and FER is French for iron, perhaps via a fire iron. A gaffer is British slang for a boss.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaffer is British informal for a boss or works foreman, the person in charge of a gang of workers.

clue.text: Pitched to cool independent film director

blocks.note: to pitch forward is to fall, so pitched means fell
what is in is fashionable or cool
I is the abbreviation for independent

explanation.surface: An independent film is pitched as cool, perhaps to a studio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitched' sounds like selling a film idea, but here it means fell.
explanation.definitionFit: Federico Fellini was the Italian director of films such as La Dolce Vita.

clue.text: Biscuit Mum takes Joey in prison

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: ma is a word for mother
the can is slang for prison
a joey is a young kangaroo, a roo

explanation.surface: Mum takes a biscuit to someone called Joey who is in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: Joey looks like a man's name, but a joey is a baby kangaroo.
explanation.definitionFit: A macaroon is a sweet biscuit made with ground almonds or coconut.

clue.text: Open University book includes chapter as a result

indicators.note: a word that includes another holds it within itself

blocks.note: the Open University is abbreviated OU
a tome is a large book
C is an abbreviation for chapter

explanation.surface: An Open University textbook includes an extra chapter as a result of something.
explanation.definitionFit: An outcome is the consequence or end product of something, so a result.

clue.text: Puts active alternative to lethargy

indicators.note: letters that are active are on the move, so they shift into a new order

blocks.note: the letters as written
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: Doing something active is offered as the alternative to lethargy.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupor is a dazed, sluggish state, close to lethargy.

clue.text: Demoted Socialist member dined in

indicators.note: these pieces placed in another sit inside it

blocks.note: a red is a socialist
a leg is a limb, a member of the body
to dine is to eat

explanation.surface: A socialist party member is demoted after dining with the wrong people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a party member, but it is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: Relegated means moved down to a lower rank or division, so demoted.

clue.text: Welcome to get soldiers in

indicators.note: the soldiers are brought in, placed inside the other word

blocks.note: taken as written
RE, the Royal Engineers, a British army corps

explanation.surface: An order to welcome the troops by letting the soldiers in.
explanation.definitionFit: To greet someone is to receive or salute them on arrival, the same as to welcome.

clue.text: Ready to fight

blocks.note: set means prepared, ready
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as one phrase, 'ready to fight', but 'Ready to' is the wordplay and 'fight' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A set-to is a brief fight or heated argument.

clue.text: Task I've managed partly to get out of doing

indicators.note: partly means only part of the words is used, a run of letters lying across them

blocks.note: the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone boasts that they managed to get out of doing part of a task.
explanation.walkthrough: To skive is British slang for dodging work or school.
explanation.definitionFit: To skive is to avoid a duty, idle out of work, so to get out of doing it.

clue.text: River is liability without oxygen, being full of toxins

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one word goes around the other

blocks.note: the Po is Italy's longest river
taken as written
an onus is a burden or responsibility
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A polluted river with no oxygen in it is a liability because it is full of toxins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without oxygen' looks like lacking oxygen, but here it means ONUS goes outside the O.
explanation.definitionFit: Something poisonous contains or produces poison, so it is full of toxins.

clue.text: The Tate, for example, has painting and really good sculpture

indicators.note: sculpture shapes material into a new form, so these letters are moulded into another order

blocks.note: a painting is a picture
taken as written, to be rearranged
G is an abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Praise for the Tate, which has fine painting and some really good sculpture.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is a group of British art museums in London and elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tate is an example of a public building where art is displayed, signalled by 'for example'.
